name: Data 101 — quiz
abstract: Ten questions to check what you learned about data.
courseDescription: Notes, a deck, and a quiz about using data to understand needs and make better decisions.

grades.name: A
grades.message: Excellent. You can ask good questions about data and explain why quality and sharing rules matter.

grades.name: B
grades.message: Strong work. Keep asking who owns the data and how good it is.

grades.name: C
grades.message: A sound start. Read the explanations, then check the notes for the ones you missed.

grades.name: D
grades.message: Go back to the key terms and the do’s and don’ts in the notes, then try again.

grades.name: F
grades.message: Start with the notes. Then take the quiz again.

questions.text: What happens when government explains how it uses data?
questions.explanation: Why it matters says the public trusts government more when it explains how it uses data.

questions.text: Which problem often keeps teams from using data well?

options.text: They cannot find, trust, or share the data they need.
The County has more storage than it can use.
Residents do not want any data collected.
Staff share too much data with the public.

questions.hint: Think about what happens when records are incomplete and owners are unclear.
questions.explanation: The Problem section says many teams cannot find, trust, or share the data they need, so leaders decide with weak evidence.

questions.text: Which action helps teams use data well?

options.text: Collect as much data as possible.
Let each team choose its own format.
Name an owner for each data set.
Check data quality only after a problem appears.

questions.hint: The first step treats data as a shared asset.
questions.explanation: The Solution section says to name an owner for each data set, check its quality, and share it under clear rules.

options.text: How much data a system can store.
How many people can see the data.
How well data fits its use.

questions.hint: Quality is about fit for a purpose.
questions.explanation: Key terms defines data quality as how well data fits its use. It can be complete, unique, consistent, timely, valid, and accurate.

questions.text: Timeliness means the data is up to date when you need it.
questions.explanation: Key terms defines timeliness as data that is up to date when you need it.

questions.text: Which term means a written deal about sharing data?
questions.hint: The answer is a written deal.
questions.explanation: Key terms defines a data sharing agreement as a written deal on what data is shared, why, and how it is protected.

questions.text: A teammate wants to share personal data first and check the rules later. What should you do?

options.text: Bring in privacy and legal staff early.
Share only half of the data.

questions.hint: Think about who should be involved early.
questions.explanation: Do’s and don’ts says to bring in privacy and legal staff early when sharing data, and not to share personal data first and check the rules later.

questions.text: It is a good idea to keep data just in case it might be useful.
questions.hint: Think about collecting only what you need.
questions.explanation: Do’s and don’ts says to collect only the data you need for a clear purpose, and not to keep data just in case.

questions.text: Which is a good question to ask about data before a decision?

options.text: Can we skip checking the data this time?
How complete, accurate, and up to date is it?

questions.hint: Think about ownership, quality, and gaps.
questions.explanation: Questions to ask includes how complete, accurate, and up to date the data is.

questions.text: What should you know before you rely on a data set?
questions.hint: Think about who is responsible for it.
questions.explanation: The Checklist includes “I know who owns the data.”
